one_liner: Rust's standard zero-copy HTTP/1.x push parser; beats picohttpparser only when pico is built without SSE4.2.
what_it_does: It parses HTTP/1.x request and response heads (method, path, version, status, reason, headers) plus chunked-encoding size lines from one contiguous &[u8]. It never allocates: the caller supplies a fixed slice of Header slots, and every field comes back as a slice borrowed from the input buffer. Each call returns Complete(offset of body), Partial (read more and re-parse the whole buffer) or an Error enum, much like picohttpparser's -2/-1 convention, but through an idiomatic Rust API (Request/Response structs, ParserConfig leniency switches) rather than the phr_* C functions.
how_it_is_fast: It validates request-target and header-value bytes with SIMD range checks (16 bytes per step in the 'sse42' path, which really uses max_epu8/cmpeq/movemask; 32 with AVX2; 16 with NEON) and finds the first delimiter with trailing_ones on the movemask, falling back to SWAR word-at-a-time checks (8 bytes in a usize using borrow tricks). On x86 with std it picks AVX2, SSE4.2 or SWAR at runtime and caches the choice in an AtomicU8, while -C target-cpu=native moves the choice to compile time and removes the dispatch branch. Smaller tricks: 'GET '/'POST' are matched as 4-byte arrays, 'HTTP/1.x' as one u64 compare, and a raw-pointer Bytes cursor skips per-byte bounds checks. It won PR #40 because picohttpparser only uses its PCMPESTRI path when compiled with __SSE4_2__ and has no runtime dispatch, and pico-sys built it without that flag.
when_to_use: You are writing or tuning a Rust HTTP/1.x server, client or proxy and need the head parsed straight out of a read buffer with zero allocations. It is the parser underneath hyper, and its crate has ~742M downloads and 551 reverse dependencies.

You ship one generic x86-64 binary: runtime dispatch picks AVX2/SSE4.2 on its own. In PR #40 that took the ~700 B browser request from 529 ns (no SIMD) to 451 ns, against 492 ns for a default-built pico.
You can build per host with -C target-cpu=native: the dispatch moves to compile time. That gave 405 ns on the same request, and 62 vs 72 ns on the short one.

no_std or embedded targets: turn off the default 'std' feature. You get the SWAR fallback, which PR #123 measured at ~20% less time per request on x86_64 and ~40% less on Apple M1 than the old byte loop.
Parsing messy real-world responses: ParserConfig can skip invalid header lines, accept obsolete line folding, and accept multiple spaces in the request/status line.
when_not_to_use: Raw speed against picohttpparser under equal build flags. The one fair-build report (issue #85: pico built with -msse4 and cross-language LTO) measured pico at ~2900 MB/s vs httparse at 1751 MB/s, and the project removed pico from its benches in 2022 (PR #112), so there has been no head-to-head since.

Scalar-only builds on realistic requests: with both parsers' SIMD off, pico won 492 vs 529 ns (PR #40) and 405 vs 468 ns (PR #38). Those numbers predate the 2023 SWAR rewrite and were never re-run against pico.
Ring buffers or scattered iovecs: parse takes a single contiguous slice (issue #74 is open), so wrapped data has to be copied first.

Slow-drip or very large header blocks: every Partial re-parses from byte 0, and there is no last_len-style resume point. The docs (added 2026-02) warn that retry loops on a growing buffer can burn CPU fast, so cap head size and time yourself.

You need HTTP semantics rather than tokenizing: it does not validate Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding, frame bodies or look up headers. For chunked bodies it only parses the size line and has no phr_decode_chunked equivalent. The URI check is a loose byte-range test (0x21-0x7E, 0x80-0xFF) followed by UTF-8 validation.

integration.dependencies: none (criterion and rand are dev-dependencies only)
integration.min_toolchain: Released v1.10.1: Rust 1.47 per CI, edition 2018, with a build.rs that probes rustc (NEON needs 1.59, otherwise SWAR). Unreleased master: rust-version 1.59, edition 2021, no build script.
integration.platforms: Any Rust target. SIMD on x86/x86_64 (SSE4.2 or AVX2, detected at runtime with std or selected at compile time via target_feature) and on aarch64 with NEON; everything else uses SWAR. CI covers x86_64 in each SIMD mode, i686-musl, aarch64 and miri. The --cfg httparse_disable_simd flag forces SWAR.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Parsing only reads the caller's buffer and writes caller-owned structs. The only global is a relaxed AtomicU8 that caches CPU-feature detection, so separate Request/Response values can be parsed concurrently.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false: it is a Rust API, not the phr_* C ABI. The model is the same (stateless, zero-copy, caller-sized header array, re-parse on partial), but there is no last_len hint and no in-place chunked decoder.

gotchas: The header slice caps the header count. One header too many returns Error::TooManyHeaders rather than Partial. On Partial, Request fields can be half-filled (method set, path None), which is by design so callers can route early.

Types are asymmetric. path is &str, so a non-UTF-8 request-target fails as Error::Token. Header values are &[u8] with trailing whitespace trimmed. A reason phrase containing obs-text comes back as "". A bare LF is accepted as a line ending.

Open issue #222 (2026-07): with allow_space_before_first_header_name(true), a whitespace-only first header line ends the head with zero headers and leaves the real headers in the buffer, a request-smuggling hazard. The option is off by default.

Pin a recent version. 1.9.5 fixed an unsound pointer::add (PR #185) and a runtime-dispatch lowering problem that had made generic x64 builds 2-10x slower on small header microbenchmarks (PR #181). 1.10.0 tightened method tokens to RFC tchar (PR #190). Before master's PR #214, no_std builds always used SWAR even with target features set. Despite the lib.rs doc, unsafe is not confined to one submodule: it appears throughout lib.rs, iter.rs and simd/, every block carries a clippy-enforced SAFETY comment, and CI runs miri and cargo-fuzz.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick httparse when you are in Rust and want the maintained, fuzzed, ecosystem-default parser with runtime SIMD dispatch and no_std support; thhp only ties pico (4421 vs 4393 MB/s with +sse4.2), and picohttpparser-rs is a C-ABI safety rewrite that wins only on header-heavy inputs. If you need a margin over picohttpparser itself, the non-Rust siblings httpp (~2.26x), http.c3l (~13%) and hparse (~12.5% wall-clock) report larger ones but are far less deployed.
verified_claims_summary: In the maintainer's PR #40 (June 2018; rustc 1.27 nightly #[bench], lto=true, an unnamed CPU with SSE4.2), a ~700 B, 10-header browser GET took 451 ns with runtime detection and 405 ns with target-cpu=native, vs 492 ns for picohttpparser built via pico-sys without SSE4.2 (~1.09x / ~1.21x); the short request was 70 and 62 ns vs 72 ns. With SIMD off httparse lost (529 vs 492 ns), and a third party's equal-flags build (issue #85) had pico ~1.66x faster.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-30, last release v1.10.1 on 2025-03-03, so master's MSRV bump and no_std SIMD are unreleased), MIT OR Apache-2.0, dependency-free and effectively the Rust HTTP/1.x default, so it is safe to adopt; its speed edge over pico is the weak part, not its maturity.
